articles.title: House Republican aims to put Democrats on the record over DSA with resolution condemning socialism
articles.summary: Jeff Crank's House resolution condemning socialism cites Zohran Mamdani's NYC mayoral win and the DSA's growing political momentum nationwide.
articles.body: Rep. Jeff Crank, R-Colo., introduced a measure Thursday condemning socialism in all its forms, telling Fox News Digital he wants to use the vote to force moderate House Democrats to take a more public stance against the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "I keep hearing people like Hakeem Jeffries and others in the Congress saying that they oppose the DSA. Let's see if they're willing to vote for a resolution that would oppose them," Crank told Fox News Digital in an interview on Friday. Crank's House resolution cites New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory as one of the clearest signposts of the DSA’s growing political momentum. A recent Brookings Institution analysis found that as of August 12, 123 candidates endorsed or recommended by national, state or local DSA chapters had won primaries this cycle. Most were running for local or state-level office. FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS Crank described the DSA movement as "anti-American" and "anti-Constitution," arguing that its members are often hostile to free speech, one of the core rights protected by the U.S. Constitution. He also accused DSA members of being anti-Semitic in their advocacy against Israel, particularly after the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. "I would almost say the DSA in some ways is the marriage between socialism, the traditional socialism of Bernie Sanders, and the anti-Semitism of this sort of radical Arab movement," Crank said. He continued: "If that's a marriage, their child is violence, right? It's violence and intimidation. It's showing up at town hall meetings and trying to shout elected officials down, which, by the way, is completely anti-democratic." MAMDANI FACES QUESTIONS OVER TIES TO OUTLET ACCUSED OF ANTISEMITIC TROPES One recent example of DSA members disrupting an elected official came in February, when San Francisco DSA led a protest at a news conference held by Mayor Daniel Lurie, who is Jewish. Lurie was announcing a tax-cut proposal when demonstrators repeatedly chanted "Tax the rich." During the disruption, a woman also shouted "tax the Jews," though DSA and other protesters said she was not affiliated with the group. Crank also took aim at several proposals contained in the DSA's national program, arguing that they undermine "free and fair elections." His House resolution calls for passage of the SAVE Act — which would require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections — while also highlighting the DSA's support for extending voting rights to "noncitizens." According to the DSA's program, all permanent U.S. residents should have the right to vote, as should incarcerated people and those with criminal convictions. CLINTON-APPOINTED JUDGE TRIGGERS APPEAL AFTER BLOCKING KEY VOTER CITIZENSHIP LAW The program also calls for abolishing the Senate and replacing the Supreme Court with "a judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress." Crank also criticized the DSA's explicit opposition to capitalism, arguing that socialism has repeatedly failed both in the United States and abroad. "I find it ironic that many of the people who are pushing socialism or who are involved in the DSA movement, they're people who came here from a different country and now they come here and want to impose... the socialism that they left, that didn't work," Crank said. He singled out Mamdani as "the first verified failure of socialism," citing his pied-à-terre tax. DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY' "You're seeing socialism at its worst in places like New York with Mamdani who's saying, 'Well, I am just going to tax anybody who has a big house here,'" Crank said. "Well, people can choose to not have a house in New York. So they leave. It doesn't work." He added: "He's the first one to sort of get elected, and now he's trying to spread it and get other DSA members around the country elected." Crank also mentioned Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old DSA member who won her Colorado primary in July after handily defeating Democratic incumbent Diana DeGette. "[Kiros] said America deserved 9/11. So tell me why that's different? When you have a bunch of terrorists on September 11th killing Americans because of ideology, how is that different than what Mao did? It isn't. This is the insidiousness of this movement," Crank said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Crank's resolution similarly draws a line between modern Democratic socialists and past communist regimes under leaders such as Mao Zedong and Joseph Stalin, asserting that socialism has led to famine, mass killings and more than 100 million deaths worldwide. Kiros' comments on 9/11 stem from an interview she did on June 22 with 9News journalist Kyle Clark, who asked her whether she believed the attacks were an "inevitable consequence" of American intervention. "Inevitable in the sense that we destabilized a lot of the Middle East, which led people to believe that another act of violence was the only response. And again, just like I said before, our responsibility is to get rid of those conditions that lead to violence in the first place," Kiros said. Crank's resolution will be considered by the House Rules Committee on Monday, and there will be a vote likely sometime next week, the congressman told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump touts access to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil in deal he says will slash gas prices
articles.summary: The Trump administration is touting the oil deal with Venezuela as a way to lower gasoline prices, which have been elevated since the Iran war broke out.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Friday touted an agreement with Venezuela that he said would lower gas prices by giving the U.S. majority control over 65 billion barrels of oil from the South American country's proven reserves. The breakthrough comes as disruptions to global energy markets from the Iran war continue to push up prices at the pump, with Americans now paying an average of $4.08 per gallon for regular gasoline, up from $3.20 a year ago, according to AAA. The agreement with Venezuela will give the U.S. a 55% effective interest in the output of a new private company formed to manage the reserves, a U.S. official familiar with the deal told The Associated Press. While the U.S. will not immediately gain access to 35.75 billion barrels of oil, the 55% interest applies to the oil ultimately produced by the 17 Venezuelan fields covered by the agreement. TRUMP PREDICTS GAS PRICES WILL GO DOWN TO $2.50 PER GALLON IF STRAIT OF HORMUZ FULLY OPENS The agreement also allows the U.S. to purchase Venezuelan oil at cost, a provision that could give American buyers access to cheaper crude once production from the fields increases. The deal is unlikely to translate into an immediate drop in U.S. gasoline prices, however, because experts have said bringing significantly more Venezuelan crude to market will require years of infrastructure work and billions of dollars in investment, according to the AP. Rystad Energy, an independent energy research firm, said in July that Venezuelan oil production could jump 17% by 2028, but only if significant advances are made. According to the firm's report, Venezuela will need "higher drilling activity, extensive workover campaigns, improved infrastructure and significantly greater rig availability." Since much of Venezuela’s crude is extremely heavy and viscous, the country also needs a steady supply of diluents — lighter hydrocarbons blended with the crude to make it thin enough to flow through pipelines and reach refineries and export terminals. In 2021, S&P Global described Venezuelan oil as having "the viscosity of asphalt." TRUMP BLASTS BIG OIL FOR ‘MAKING TOO MUCH MONEY’ The U.S. Energy Information Administration has also previously weighed in on Venezuela's troubled oil industry. In October 2023, after the Biden administration lifted most U.S. sanctions on Venezuela's oil sector, the agency said "years of underinvestment and mismanagement" would limit growth. The Trump administration, however, is betting that U.S. involvement and a massive influx of private investment can reverse the decline. Trump said Friday the new agreement would greatly increase the U.S. oil supply and "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Secretary of State Marco Rubio similarly said the deal would bring nearly $100 billion in private investment to Venezuela and lower gas prices in the United States. U.S. oil companies have been cautious about investing in Venezuela, citing the country’s deteriorated infrastructure and uncertain business environment. Days after the Trump administration ousted Nicolás Maduro, Trump met with oil executives to discuss potential investment in Venezuela’s energy sector, but several expressed reservations. ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said at the time that he viewed Venezuela as "un-investable." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: German AfD youth group eyes euro stance at congress ahead of key polls
articles.summary: The youth wing of the Alternative for Germany party met for a national congress on Saturday, ahead of a key election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt th...
articles.body:
The youth wing of the Alternative for Germany party met for a national congress on Saturday, ahead of a key election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt that could see the far-right AfD take power for the first time.

At the event in the eastern city of Magdeburg, the Generation Deutschland (GD) youth organization discussed its stance on European policy, aiming to distance itself from the main party's line.

Its lead candidate for the Saxony-Anhalt election, Ulrich Siegmund, was met with energetic approval by the delegates.

The approximately 300 participants discussed a statement at the 'Altes Theater' theatre in Magdeburg.

A draft of the statement, which had been made public beforehand, stated that the euro had strengthened the single market but had significant structural flaws. For this reason, they were open to proposals for reform. There is no talk of leaving the euro.

GD leader Jean-Pascal Hohm said that he personally was firmly convinced that Germany should not leave the euro.

However, Hohm ultimately withdrew the relevant motion put forward by the GD leadership after it became clear from speeches that there was significant resistance within the AfD Youth to such a stance.

The AfD was founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic party. In its 2025 Bundestag election manifesto, it had reaffirmed that "Germany must leave the euro system."

Hohm justified his stance by referring to the way of life of young people, who are used to no longer having to show a passport at borders or convert currencies, he said in remarks to dpa.

'Millions must leave this country again'

At its meeting, the GD appeared extremely self-assured and reiterated calls for mass deportations. "Germany must remain the land of the Germans. This principle is non-negotiable," Hohm asserted. Millions had entered the country, he claimed. "Millions must leave this country again."

Hohm also called on members to defend themselves physically in the event of physical attacks by political opponents.

He does not expect anyone to allow themselves to be "beaten up by violence-seeking anti-fascists or chased through the city" because of their political convictions.

Anyone who defends themselves in a situation of self-defence has the backing of the GD and the parent party. "We are not victims, and we will not allow ourselves to be made into victims."

The GD, which is closely linked to its parent party, was newly founded in Giessen last year after the former AfD youth organization, the Junge Alternative (JA), had been dissolved. The JA was a largely independent association over which the AfD had only limited control.

The meeting was heavily influenced by the election campaign. Referring to the upcoming state election on September 6, Hohm said that history could be made in Saxony-Anhalt next week.

Siegmund, who arrived in the afternoon, was celebrated like a pop star. "The people are on our side," he called out to the participants.

He said he had often heard the word "hope" in recent weeks. "We will make history here in Saxony-Anhalt one way or another."

Siegmund emphasized that he remained optimistic even if the AfD were to fall short of the absolute majority it was aiming for. "Then it'll work out soon in Thuringia, then in Brandenburg, then in Saxony," he called out to the cheering hall.

According to a spokesman, 480 participants, guests and journalists were invited to GD's second national congress.

The police put the number of the group's own participants at 300, while counter-demonstrations on Saturday remained limited in scale, with the police citing around 250 participants before the start of the event.

There were no significant counterdemonstrations of the sort that took place when the GD was founded last year in Giessen.

According to the police, a total of around 600 people took part in demonstrations and rallies against the Federal Congress, the AfD and racism throughout the day at various locations across the city. From the police's point of view, everything remained peaceful.

Due to their anti-constitutional views, the AfD chapters in Saxony-Anhalt and three other eastern states - Thuringia, Saxony and Brandenburg - are classified as "confirmed" right-wing extremist movements by intelligence agencies, allowing for the party to be monitored by authorities.

Nevertheless, the party has soared in popularity in recent years, benefiting from discontent with the political establishment in Berlin, and it is polling above 40% in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of the vote on September 6.

All mainstream parties refuse to work with the AfD, a policy famously known as the "firewall," but successive governments have rejected calls for the party to be banned due to its extremist positions.

articles.title: Dem House hopeful’s delayed disclosure reveals mystery payments from Soros-linked groups
articles.summary: Rebecca Cooke's financial disclosure reveals she was compensated by two organizations with direct ties to George Soros' Open Society Foundation.
articles.body: A waitress running for Congress in Wisconsin's third district was on the payroll of two left-leaning organizations with ties to billionaire investor George Soros' Open Society Foundation. Rebecca Cooke has portrayed herself as a working-class outsider, touting her experience as a waitress, small-business owner and nonprofit leader raised on a dairy farm. But a personal financial disclosure released two days after Wisconsin’s Aug. 13 primary shows she received more than $5,000 apiece for work with Third Way and the Pipeline Fund, two left-leaning organizations with financial ties to George Soros’ Open Society network. The Open Society network awarded $1 million to Third Way’s nonprofit research arm between 2023 and 2024, while the Pipeline Fund received $1.4 million directly from the Open Society Action Fund in 2024. Through the Open Society Foundation, which serves as the umbrella organization for Soros' philanthropy network, Soros has distributed tens of millions of dollars to nonprofits and groups championing left-leaning causes like policing reform, LGBTQ rights and drug decriminalization. Soros has donated more than $32 billion of his personal fortune to the Open Society's Foundation, which has been overseen by his son Alex Soros since 2022. DEMOCRATIC GROUP LAUNCHES $15M WAR ON DSA AFTER SOCIALIST PRIMARY WINS: 'MORTAL DANGER' The financial disclosure forms only report that the amount of money Cooke received from each organization was above $5,000, but they do not specify the exact amount. The personal financial disclosure form covered Jan. 1, 2025, through July 14, 2026. A spokesperson for Third Way confirmed with Fox News Digital reporting by the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Cooke received $30,000 in payment "for a project focused on elevating the voices and concerns of working-class Americans that have too often been missing from the rooms where decisions are made." The Foundation to Promote Open Society, a grant making arm of George Soros’ Open Society Foundations network, donated a $500,000 grant to the Third Way Institute in 2023 and another one in 2024, according to IRS-derived grant records. Third Way Institute serves as the 501(c) research arm of the Third Way. In 2024, Third Way Institute transferred $21.9 million to Third Way, accounting for roughly 98% of the institute’s total spending that year. The institute said the money was used to support charitable and educational work on economic, national security, energy and social policy issues. SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES Fox News Digital reached out to Third Way for comment. Pipeline Fund is a organization that works to train, recruit and support progressive candidates running in state and local election races. It began operating independently in 2024 after spinning off from the Sixteen Thirty Fund, a liberal nonprofit network that has received tens of millions of dollars from the Soros-founded Open Society network. Tax records also show that the Pipeline Fund received $1.4 million directly from the Open Society Action Fund and approximately $2.26 million from the Sixteen Thirty Fund in 2024. Scattered across the country, Pipeline Fund has a network of campaign consulting groups, including one in Wisconsin known as Wisconsin Progress. "We can confirm Rebecca Cooke worked as a contractor for The Pipeline Fund in 2025 to help advance our mission of building a reflective democracy where working-class people, women, people of color, and other underrepresented communities are fully supported to run for office and advance the needs of their communities," Pipeline Fund said in an emailed statement to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. HOUSE DEMOCRATS' CAMPAIGN ARM DRAWS PROGRESSIVE FURY FOR TRYING TO 'TIP THE SCALES' IN KEY HOUSE PRIMARY Prior to making a bid for Congress herself, Cooke opened up her own Democratic campaign consulting firm in 2015, in which she worked with eight state and federal campaigns from 2015 to 2021. "Radical Rebecca Cooke is a paid political operative for far-left liberals and wants to push their socialist agenda. Commie Cooke may fit in at [a] Soros-funded consulting firm, but she is far too extreme to represent western Wisconsin," National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Zach Bannon said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Cooke’s personal financial disclosure was not released until two days after the Aug. 13 primary, following an extension she requested from the clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives in April. All candidates who spend or raise more than $5,000 for a House of Representatives race must submit a personal financial disclosure form 30 days before the election. Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., blasted Cooke's delay in releasing her financial records, saying it tells voters all they need to know about her. "For months, Democrats and Republicans across the Third District called on Cooke to release her financial disclosures. She had every opportunity to be transparent with voters. Instead, she chose to keep them hidden until after the primary," Van Orden said in a news release. DEMOCRAT ESTABLISHMENT STRIKES BACK AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATE DOWNED IN BATTLEGROUND PRIMARY "That tells Wisconsin voters everything they need to know about Rebecca Cooke’s character. She was willing to deceive her own party to protect the political persona she built and gain political power," Van Orden said. But Cooke said her financial forms reveal that she truly is a working-class American. "I’ve always worn multiple hats to make ends meet and in addition to waitressing I worked on two projects related to getting more working class people to run for office and conducted research for an organization about how to better connect with working class voters," Cooke said in an email to the Sentinel. "There are unique challenges to running for office as a working class person with an hourly wage job and a full-time campaign schedule. For example, I’m one of the thousands of people in this district who can’t afford health insurance. I’ve been proud to help make it easier for the next generation of working class leaders to step up and take our fight to Washington D.C." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached to Open Society Foundation, Cooke's campaign and Pipeline Fund for comment.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed plays down Hasan Piker ties after streamer’s viral antisemitism firestorm
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed tried to downplay his ties to Hasan Piker on air, but Katy Tur pressed him on why he won't fully disassociate ahead of a tight race.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed tried to turn the page on his ties to controversial streamer Hasan Piker Friday — but MS NOW host Katy Tur pushed back. The candidate’s comments come just days after Piker suggested Jewish Americans are "making antisemitism worse" by voicing their support of Israel — a statement that drew harsh criticism from El-Sayed, who has appeared alongside Piker on the campaign trail. "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed said in a statement following Piker’s remarks. EL-SAYED DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER DISTURBING REMARKS ABOUT JEWISH AMERICANS He added that "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms," while promising to "stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk." "And while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools and healthcare," El-Sayed continued. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT DEMANDS REPORTERS STOP ASKING 'ABOUT HASAN PIKER' AHEAD OF SENATE RACE On Friday’s "The Moment with Katy Tur," El-Sayed appeared to continue his effort to distance himself from Piker in light of his controversial remarks. "So, if you have Jewish voters in Michigan — I’ll say [Attorney General] Dana Nessel is one of them — who are worried about your association with Hasan Piker. Why? Why keep him so close? Or why not fully disassociate yourself with him, especially when Michigan is so tight? Elissa Slotkin only won by 22,000 votes," Tur asked. According to Ballotpedia, Slotkin won by 19,000 votes. MICHIGAN DEM AG TURNS ON EL-SAYED OVER TERROR ATTACK RESPONSE, WARNS OF MENTALITY THAT 'BOTHERS ME A LOT' "This campaign is not about a streamer in California. This campaign is about affordability in Michigan. This campaign is about the ability to have healthcare," El-Sayed said. Tur pushed back, arguing the "streamer in California does campaign with a lot of Democrats. So he’s not just a streamer." HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS El-Sayed appeared to continue distancing himself from Piker, despite Tur’s pushback. "This campaign is about the challenges Michiganders face," El-Sayed continued. "And I get that, in the media, it’s a lot easier to pick up one person and be like, ‘This is what this is about.’ But this is why a lot of people get so frustrated about politics and political media, because it doesn’t actually speak to the challenges they face." WISCONSIN DEMOCRAT DOWNPLAYS APPEARING ON HASAN PIKER'S SHOW, DOESN'T 'ENDORSE' EVERYTHING HE SAYS The exchange continued, with Tur rejecting El-Sayed’s characterization of his public ties to Piker. "It’s not just the media, and I reject that framing," Tur said. "It’s — six in 10 Americans don’t know who he is, and I’m not saying he’s the most important person in the world. But when you have a state like Michigan, where, again, Elissa Slotkin only won by 22,000 votes, is it worth potentially losing the few votes you need to win?" "Ten in 10 Americans agree that they can’t afford the things that they need in their lives," El-Sayed replied. "So, if folks want to make this about a streamer in California, they’re welcome to do that. But I’m focused on Donald Trump. I’m focused on addressing the affordability crisis. I’m focused on getting you healthcare. And that’s what I’m going to stay focused on." FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY' El-Sayed’s apparent distance himself from Piker drew criticism from Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, who told Fox News Digital his attempts to distance himself from Piker could do more harm than good to his campaign. "Distancing yourself from someone’s comments rarely works," Mudd said. "Owning your own position does. The moment a candidate argues about how close a relationship is, the audience stops listening to the substance and starts watching the deflection." ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK "If this were my client, I would advise them to skip the minimizing and go straight to a clear, standalone statement: here’s what I believe, separate from what anyone else said," Mudd continued. "Ambiguity is what keeps a story alive, not the original comment." Mudd added that El-Sayed’s strategy should be to double-down on his own campaign promises and personal beliefs, instead of just claiming he disagrees with Piker’s statements. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The test isn’t whether a candidate can prove distance from a controversial figure," Mudd told Fox News Digital. "It’s whether their own answer sounds confident, consistent, and complete the first time. Reporters don’t stop asking follow-up questions. Vague answers do." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, a representative for El-Sayed pointed to a story in The Hill reporting that the candidate has "no plans" to campaign with Piker. Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment.

articles.title: Seneca Nation leader calls Trump's Lake America renaming 'unpresidential,' demands reversal
articles.summary: Seneca Nation's leader calls Trump's Lake Ontario to Lake America renaming "unpresidential," saying it violates the 1794 Canandaigua treaty.
articles.body: A day after President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid a trade war with Canada, the leader of Seneca Nation of Indians asked him to reverse it. Calling his order "unpresidential," president J. Conrad Seneca on Friday wrote: "The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action. His order should be rescinded, and the name Lake Ontario should be left as it is, reflective of the Seneca people, other Haudenosaunee nations and all Indigenous people surrounding the lake." Seneca explained that the lake derived its name from Indigenous roots. TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT "In our traditional Seneca language, its name is sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning ‘beautiful lake,’" he wrote in a message shared in the nation’s newsletter. "Long before the United States existed, and before settlers brought the English language to our lands, our Seneca and Haudenosaunee ancestors traveled Lake Ontario and surrounding waterways for many reasons, including diplomacy among our nations. Now, we are seeing the exact opposite of diplomacy." He added that to the people of Seneca Nation, Lake America is not a "political pawn" but rather land that Indigenous people have lived on for thousands of years. HILLARY CLINTON'S DIG AT TRUMP OVER LAKE ONTARIO NAME CHANGE SPARKS VIRAL BACKLASH: 'SHOOTING BLANKS' "The action that President Trump is taking is starkly un-presidential and demeaning to his office and his standing as the leader of the free world," Seneca argued. "His blatant disrespect toward the Seneca people, other Haudenosaunee nations, and all Indigenous people is unacceptable." He noted that first President George Washington signed a treaty with several nations, including the Seneca, in 1794 "promising to live in peace and friendship with one another." "The United States also promised our people the free use and enjoyment of our lands forever," Seneca said. "President Trump’s aggression toward our culture with his Executive Order violates that peace, friendship and commitments of the Canandaigua treaty." "This is the latest in a long history of willful attempts to disregard the United States’ commitments to the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee nations," he continued. "President Trump needs to be reminded of those commitments." He added that Article 6 of the U.S. Constitution "clearly states that treaties are the ‘supreme Law of the Land,’ and need to always be honored as such." HOUSE DEM'S 'LAKE NATALIE' JAB AT TRUMP AIDE SETS SOCIAL MEDIA ABLAZE: 'STAY CLASSY' Seneca called on all Native groups and federal, state and local representatives — "regardless of political party" — to stand against the name change. "We will always call Lake Ontario by the name derived from the language of our ancestors — the name that, like the strength and influence of the Seneca people, will live on forever, long after the intrusive political tirades of individual men," he said. ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES Trump announced the name change on Thursday. "The Lake of America was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually," he told reporters while signing the Executive Order in the Oval Office. "As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico — we changed it — and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Trump said in the Oval Office." TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS The president said he had directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the department to update the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the name change. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the name change on X, writing, "The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always." VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY' The move to rename the lake, which sits on the U.S.-Canada border, came amid a breakdown in trade between both nations, with Trump accusing Ottawa of unfair trade practices. Trump floated renaming the lake hours before Carney's announcement of reciprocal tariffs on U.S. imports. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED The U.S. imposed new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods such as wine, furniture and dairy products, while Carney said U.S. trade demands proved Washington wanted to "destroy our major industries," including autos, steel and aluminum, FOX Business previously reported. "Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade," Trump said Thursday. "Very sadly, even the military, you know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don't get anything. They don't pay us to defend Canada." Trump also jokingly floated renaming the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. "So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," he said. "Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both." Trump previously used geographic names to make political statements, ordering the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Trump’s executive order has been criticized by several governors, including Democrats New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers and Republican Vermont Gov. Phil Scott. "New York won’t be calling it that," Hochul wrote on X. Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Michigan, announced that she plans to introduce House legislation that would nullify the change. "Donald Trump can sign all the executive orders he wants, but it will always be Lake Ontario," she wrote in a press release. "Canada is not our enemy. It is our neighbor, our ally, and one of Michigan’s most important economic partners. It is a friendship that no stroke of a pen can erase." articles.title: Leavitt is leaving the White House. Don’t expect her to go far
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt wrapped up her final day as White House press secretary on Thursday, but she is not expected to veer far from President Trump’s orbit as Republicans seek to defend their majorities on Capitol Hill. Trump and Leavitt announced earlier this month she would depart the White House to spend more time with her…
articles.body:
Karoline Leavitt wrapped up her final day as White House press secretary on Thursday, but she is not expected to veer far from President Trump’s orbit as Republicans seek to defend their majorities on Capitol Hill.

Trump and Leavitt announced earlier this month she would depart the White House to spend more time with her young children, but both said she would serve as an outside adviser to the president. The former press secretary also confirmed last week that she would work at Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc.

While Leavitt will no longer be front and center at the White House podium, she will likely continue to play a significant role having Trump’s ear and crafting his messaging on the campaign trail.

“While she’s a warrior, she understands the base and how to break through the legacy news media cycle,” Republican strategist Ford O’Connell said.

“Ahead of the most consequential midterms for Republicans, a warrior with that kind of skillset is invaluable to the president and to the Republican Party,” he continued.

The admiration for Leavitt among Trump’s base is evident at the president’s campaign events.

Leavitt was met with a standing ovation last week in Myrtle Beach, S.C., during Trump’s rally for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.).

“She’s fantastic,” Trump told his supporters.

The trip marked Leavitt’s last trip with Trump as press secretary. However, Leavitt said on Air Force One that she will travel with Trump to the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas next month.

“You guys will see me all the time,” Leavitt told reporters.

Leavitt brings a unique set of skills to the table as an outside adviser. In addition to her experience as White House press secretary, Leavitt served as Trump’s campaign spokesperson in 2024 and was a spokesperson for MAGA Inc. before that.

The former press secretary also has experience as a candidate herself, having run for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District against incumbent Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) in 2022.

“She has a rare combination of proximity to the president, the White House and the campaign trail,” O’Connell said.

Leavitt’s departure comes as Republicans are facing a daunting national environment in the final months of the campaign as Trump’s approval sinks and Democrats hold a lead on the generic ballot.

Trump’s approval rating hit a record low of 33 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released earlier this week. Meanwhile, a poll released by Emerson College and The Hill last week showed Democrats leading Republicans by 8 points on a generic ballot.

“The House is much harder to hold, but the Senate is an area with particularly her knowledge of the base, it could be very valuable,” O’Connell said.

Leavitt addressed concerns over the headwinds Republicans face going into November during some of her final public remarks as press secretary on Thursday, vowing that Trump will continue to “push his message until the very last day” of the campaign.

“Democrats in this town want to talk a lot about affordability, but they voted against the largest tax cuts in American history,” Leavitt said. “They voted against putting more money in Americans’ pockets.”

Trump’s campaign travel and MAGA Inc.’s public activity are already ramping up ahead of the midterms.

The super PAC announced this week that Vice President Vance will travel to battleground Michigan to boost Republican candidates in the state next week.

“MAGA Inc. will be hosting events throughout the nation to ensure that Republicans retain control of Congress in order to finish cleaning up the mess the Biden-Harris-Pelosi-Schumer Democrats left,” MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said in a Thursday statement.

“We’re not going back to their record inflation, open borders, and surging crime,” Pfeiffer said.

And Trump headlined a Republican National Committee fundraiser in battleground Texas on Thursday evening.

There are a number of avenues Leavitt, who just turned 29, can take in her career after the White House.

Two of her recent predecessors: Kayleigh McEnany, who served as press secretary for Trump in his first term, and Jen Psaki, former President Biden’s first press secretary, have both taken on television hosting gigs, while Sarah Huckabee Sanders, another former Trump press secretary, went on to successfully run for Arkansas governor.

Experts say they would not be surprised if Leavitt considered another run for public office down the line.

“As a young woman who has clearly had aspirations for holding office and we know has the resources to run for office, and obviously has tremendous connections for resources to run for office. I mean, why wouldn’t she think about that down the road?” said Debbie Walsh, the director for the Center for American Women in Politics at Rutgers University.

articles.title: James Carville predicts a 2028 'reckoning' as socialist candidates eye the Democratic ticket
articles.summary: James Carville says Democratic voters won't nominate a DSA-aligned candidate in 2028, even as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez renews her membership.
articles.body: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville said the Democratic Party faces an ideological "reckoning" in 2028 but rejected the idea that primary voters will choose a Democratic socialist presidential nominee. Speaking on "Saturday in America," Carville offered his prediction for how Democratic voters will approach the party's 2028 presidential primary. "The reckoning will be in a nominating process for the nominee of the Democratic Party in 2028. This has to be taken to Democratic voters," Carville said while discussing recent victories by candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY WILL TEST TRUE STRENGTH OF PARTY'S SOCIALIST WING As DSA-backed candidates have won races across the country, some centrist Democrats have raised concerns about the group's growing influence. Carville argued that Democratic voters won't nominate a DSA-aligned presidential candidate in 2028. "Let me assure you that Democratic voters are not going to nominate the DSA or anybody close to the DSA. The Democrats have never nominated the most liberal candidate, and they're not [going to] do it in 2028," he said. CARVILLE SAYS ONE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST'S 'LUNACY OF THE HIGHEST LEVEL' POLICY COULD HAUNT SWING-STATE DEMS Despite Carville's prediction about 2028, several DSA-backed candidates have secured primary victories this year, with notable wins in New York and Colorado. High-profile elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, are also affiliated with the group. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., recently renewed her DSA membership following a seven-year lapse and has been discussed as a potential 2028 presidential contender. 2028 BATTLEGROUND POLL SCRAMBLES DEMOCRATS' FUTURE AS INSURGENT SOCIALIST SEIZES LEAD "First of all, she has more talent than most of the people on the left put together. And I put her in an entirely different category," Carville said of Ocasio-Cortez. "She's a very talented, very articulate person," he said, adding that the DSA is going to "run somebody for president in 2028, and they're not going to get out of the first two primaries." Carville said the party will "move forward" but concluded that the DSA is a "minor part of the Democratic coalition." AOC BLASTED AS TOO MODERATE BY MAOIST DSA FACTION AS 2028 BUZZ GROWS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The DSA confirmed Ocasio-Cortez's renewed membership in a statement shared with City & State New York. "Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026," the DSA wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment but did not immediately hear back.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed peppered with questions on Hasan Piker link, fracture with Jewish Dems at Michigan convention
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed dodged four reporter questions about Hasan Piker at Michigan's Democratic convention, dismissing the streamer as irrelevant to his race.
articles.body: LANSING, Mich. — Socialist-adjacent Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed addressed the media during Saturday's state Democratic Party Nominating Convention, where he was dogged by many of the same questions that have plagued his campaign for months. Surrounded by media in a hallway at the Lansing Center, where the convention took place, El-Sayed was peppered with questions from the press about his relationship with far-left online personality Hasan Piker, along with his stance on Israel and Gaza, which has driven a wedge between his campaign and some Democrats, especially Jewish ones. "We’re in the state of Michigan. If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat," El-Sayed told reporters. "This is about affordability in Michigan. This is about seeing a doctor in Michigan. This is about Donald Trump’s disastrous policies in Michigan. That’s what I’m focused on right now." ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM Four different reporters asked El-Sayed about Piker, with whom he campaigned and partied during his primary race. He dodged all of them, falling back on describing the polarizing streamer as "a streamer from California" who is irrelevant to his race in Michigan. "I am not interested in a conversation about a social media person in California. And to folks who want to make this about a social media person in California, let’s not forget what actually matters in our politics, what our politics are really about," he said. "I don’t ever want my comments to hurt anybody’s feelings. It’s important to me that people understand that I take serious the pain of all communities in this state. But I don’t want to have a conversation about a Twitch streamer in California. This is not a serious conversation." EL-SAYED DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER DISTURBING REMARKS ABOUT JEWISH AMERICANS Piker is known for saying "America deserved 9/11," praising Mao Zedong and Communist China, arguing that capitalists should be murdered in the streets and making a litany of antisemitic comments. Fox News Digital asked El-Sayed about a recent controversy stemming from comments he made in March in response to an attack on a Michigan synagogue, when federal investigators say a gunman inspired and radicalized by Hezbollah crashed into the place of worship seeking to kill as many Jewish people as he could. "Hurt people, hurt people," he said in response to the attack. He has been criticized by members of his own Party, including Secretary of State Dana Nessel, who discussed the comments in a recent interview with The Atlantic, and declined to attend Saturday's convention partly over concerns of anti-Semitism in the Democratic Party. JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS El-Sayed told Fox News Digital his comments "might have been misconstrued to be justifying something I did not intend to justify," but then offered an apology. "To anybody who feels like my comments may have been hurtful, I’m really sorry. That was not my intention. We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright," El-Sayed told Fox News Digital. "What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain." JEWISH AG’S CONVENTION BOYCOTT EXPOSES DEEPENING ISRAEL FAULT LINE AMONG MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS He also said it was the responsibility of the Democratic Party to come together. Michigan Democrats swarmed the convention center Saturday afternoon, where the theme was "unity" amid the controversies faced by the state's highest-profile candidate for elected office. articles.title: Bill Maher ridicules liberals’ 'Lake America' outrage with jab at left-wing language police

articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher mocked liberals for crying foul over President Donald Trump’s decision to rename Lake Ontario, suggesting they know a thing or two about changing things to fit a political agenda. In Friday’s opening monologue of HBO’s "Real Time," host Maher poked fun at Trump’s renaming of one of the Great Lakes to "Lake America" during an ongoing trade war with Canada. "Trump is so mad at Canada he renamed Lake Ontario Lake America," Maher said. "Now I gotta buy a new globe again." TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT "It’s like the fifth time it’s happened," Maher added, referring to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." Trade talks between the two countries crumbled late Friday as the United States moved forward with 50% tariffs on Canada. VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY' Maher then took aim at liberal outrage over the president’s decision, suggesting critics of Trump’s move had embraced politically driven changes in terminology themselves. "The liberals are very pissed at this," Maher quipped, adding, "They say you can’t just go around changing things to fit your political agenda. Just ask any Latinx birthing person." MAHER MOCKS LIBERALS FOR STILL PANICKING ABOUT TRUMP'S ANTICS, PERSONALITY AFTER 10 YEARS Trump signed the executive order renaming the lake from the Oval Office on Thursday, telling reporters, "This is official, effective immediately." Maher’s criticism was echoed by NewsBusters Managing Editor Curtis Houck, who told Fox News Digital that liberals’ willingness to embrace new terminology undermines their criticism of Trump’s latest decision. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The fact that 'Latinx' and 'birthing person' are increasingly accepted as a punchline rather than a serious demographic statement should give all of us hope that ‘Woke One’ is dead and we're never going back to that farcical time," Houck told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If only the liberal, elitist media could more consistently get the picture," he continued. "The left needs to take a seat before they can say anything about anything being renamed." The sentiment was echoed by NewsBusters Executive Editor Tim Graham. "Liberals want to rename all kinds of things to satisfy their urge for wokeness," Graham told Fox News Digital. "Just in this decade, they've pulled down all kinds of statues and renamed scads of military bases. What they hate is anything Trump does to add a patriotic pro-America tinge to something which they associate more with his ego than with patriotism. They see red – as in a red MAGA cap." "The media routinely genuflect ethnic and LGBTQ pressure groups and their demands to remake the language we're all supposed to use," he continued. "So they can't seriously object to renaming things. They just want to be the only people who get to rename things."

articles.title: Dems face uphill battle in challenge to Georgia Congressional map under new SCOTUS rules
articles.summary: Biden branded Georgia's election law "Jim Crow," and now the state's redistricting maps face a tougher legal test after the Supreme Court's Callais ruling.
articles.body: Then-President Joe Biden put Georgia at the center of the national voting-rights fight in 2021 when he branded the state’s Republican-backed election overhaul "Jim Crow in the 21st century." Now, five years later, a separate Georgia voting-rights battle involving allegations of racial discrimination is garnering national attention as it plays out in federal court. This time, the dispute centers on the state’s redrawn Congressional and state maps redrawn in 2021, with challengers facing a significantly tougher burden of proof following the Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais. The latest development came when the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court judgment striking down Georgia’s 2021 maps and returned the case to U.S. District Judge Steve Jones. The appeals court instructed Jones to reconsider the challenge under the new framework established in Callais, which raised the bar for plaintiffs alleging racial discrimination in redistricting. Under that standard, evidence that a map weakened Black voters’ electoral influence is not enough by itself. Plaintiffs must present evidence supporting a "strong inference" of intentional racial discrimination and distinguish the effects of race from those of partisan politics. SUPREME COURT RULES ON KEY VOTING RIGHTS ACT RULE AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS WAGE REDISTRICTING WAR That distinction is especially important in Georgia, where Black voters overwhelmingly support Democratic candidates, creating significant overlap between race and partisan affiliation. That overlap could make it more difficult for the challengers to prove that race, rather than political advantage, drove the district lines. Black voters and voting-rights organizations filed three lawsuits challenging the maps between December 2021 and January 2022, arguing that the districts diluted Black voting power in violation of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Jones ruled for the challengers in 2023 and ordered Georgia to create additional majority-Black districts, including one Congressional district, two state Senate districts and five state House districts. Georgia subsequently enacted replacement maps that satisfied Jones’ order while preserving the Republican Party’s political advantage elsewhere. Those maps were used in the 2024 elections and remain in place for the 2026 election cycle, while the legality of the original maps remained at the center of Georgia’s appeal. MEDIA OUTRAGE OVER SUPREME COURT’S VOTING RIGHTS ACT DECISION COLLIDES WITH REALITY Before Callais, plaintiffs suing based on Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could win their case without proving that lawmakers intentionally discriminated on the basis of race. Courts focused heavily on whether a map had the effect of diminishing minority voters’ ability to elect their preferred candidates. But under Callais, courts must more closely examine whether present-day racial discrimination was behind the redrawing of the maps rather than political advantages. Hans von Spakovsky, a senior fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said he does not believe the Georgia challenge will survive the new test. "I don’t think a challenge will succeed because there is no evidence of current racial discrimination going on in the state legislature," von Spakovsky said. "Prior rulings against the state were based on judges misconstruing and misinterpreting Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by claiming there was racial dilution resulting from partisan gerrymandering." "That is not the correct legal standard under Section 2," he continued. "Partisan gerrymandering is constitutional and is not a violation of Section 2." GEORGIA REDISTRICTING BATTLE REVIVED AFTER APPEALS COURT OVERTURNS FEDERAL COURT DECISION Georgia can argue that lawmakers were pursuing partisan objectives rather than targeting Black voters because of their race. Because the state’s Black and Democratic voting blocs substantially overlap, separating those possible motivations could prove difficult for the challengers. "The Supreme Court in the Callais decision specifically said that a viable claim under Section 2 can only be shown if there is evidence of current racial discrimination, and judges must distinguish between racial and political bases for the way people vote," von Spakovsky said. "In other words, there’s no racial dilution going on when individuals are voting a particular way because of their politics," he added. Jones must now decide how to handle the remanded case. The plaintiffs could ask to supplement the record with revised maps, updated statistical analyses or additional evidence addressing the Supreme Court’s new requirements. The 11th Circuit, however, did not automatically grant them a new trial or authorize them to rebuild their case from the beginning. Georgia could argue that the plaintiffs already received a full trial and that Jones should apply the new standard solely to the existing record. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Whatever Jones decides is unlikely to alter Georgia’s districts before the November 2026 midterm elections. The appeals court did not order the state to reinstate the original 2021 maps, and Georgia has already conducted its primaries using the replacement districts created from the 2023 map.

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump admin economic tensions leave GOP vulnerable; U.S. foreign relations shift
articles.summary: Republicans are nearing the final stretch of the midterm election cycle with an increasingly unstable political landscape, as races for traditionally safe red seats grow competitive amid tensions over President Trump’s economic agenda. Democrats are looking to flip a handful of key battleground states to regain a Congressional majority come November. Senate races in Texas,…
articles.body:
Republicans are nearing the final stretch of the midterm election cycle with an increasingly unstable political landscape, as races for traditionally safe red seats grow competitive amid tensions over President Trump’s economic agenda.

Democrats are looking to flip a handful of key battleground states to regain a Congressional majority come November. Senate races in Texas, Iowa and Alaska, states Trump won decisively in 2024, have ticked left. The same goes for open congressional seats in North Carolina, Maine and Ohio.

With Trump’s declining approval ratings, as well as the public’s growing doubt surrounding the Iran war, rising prices and immigration enforcement, Democrats have become increasingly optimistic that some current Republican-held seats are within reach.

Despite the president’s approval dip, Trump and Republican leaders are leaning onto his favorability among his base as they attempt to curb a potential turnout drop. Trump urged supporters this week to “pretend” he’s on the ballot in November, a talking point echoed by other allies.

In the battle for Texas’ Senate seat, Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who defeated longtime Sen. John Cornyn (R) in the May primary, is locked in a tight race against state Rep. James Talarico (D).

Several surveys have shown the two candidates are neck and neck. An Emerson College poll showed Paxton at 47 percent and Talarico at 46 percent, while others placed the Democrat narrowly ahead.

Talarico entered the race with a massive fundraising advantage, raising more than $31 million compared to Paxton’s $9.3 million, according to campaign finance records.

The approaching elections have also placed the battle over mail-in voting in the spotlight.

The Justice Department on Friday appealed a temporary block on new U.S. Postal Service regulations governing mail ballots, extending a lengthy back-and-forth between Democratic states and the Trump administration over the rules — set to be in place for the November elections.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani on Thursday temporarily barred the administration from implementing portions of the regulation, siding with Democratic-led states and voting rights groups challenging them.

Talwani agreed that it would be “practically impossible” for states to comply with the rule, which required them to submit lists of all eligible voters 90 days before the November if they want to receive mail in ballots.

The judge argued the short timeline would create an “overwhelming risk” that voters who rely on mail ballots could be disenfranchised.

The Trump administration in its appeal pushed back on the claim that the federal government was attempting to take control of elections, saying the rule’s requirements were “modest.”

Trump, meanwhile, is battling a trade war with Canada after negotiations between the two longtime allies broke down.

A 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect last week, prompting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to impose “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs beginning Sept. 8.

Trump, in turn, raised the stakes again Monday, threatening to impose 50 percent tariffs on Canadian automobiles, auto parts and steel starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Amid tariff battle, the president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario — shared between Ottawa and the state of New York — to “Lake America.”

The dispute threatens to raise costs on both sides of the border. U.S. goods and services traded with Canada totaled an estimated $872 billion in 2025, and major supply chains are deeply integrated between the two nations.

The economic confrontation with Canada comes as the Trump administration simultaneously tackles economic pressure in its nearly six-month war with Iran.

After Trump threatened an “economic D-Day” against Tehran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced Operation Economic Outcast — an effort to pressure countries around the world to cut financial ties with Iran or risk losing access to the U.S. dollar system.

It’s the latest attempt from the administration to pressure Tehran into a deal after months of military action and diplomatic conversations have failed to end the conflict.

A June memorandum of understanding signed by the U.S. and Iran fell apart last month, while efforts to reach an agreement over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have stalled.

The administration’s focus on Iran unfolds alongside major policy shifts regarding Venezuela.

Trump announced Friday night that the U.S. reached a deal giving it majority control over a portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves, which he said would increase American supplies and eventually lower gas prices — which have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) said Saturday she believes the ongoing legal battle over the Kennedy Center could stand in the way of President Trump tearing down the building, after his administration raised demolition as a possibility earlier this week.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the center’s board who has successfully challenged Trump’s proposed changes to the performing arts center in court, was asked in an interview what would stop Trump from demolishing the building.

“If Donald Trump and the administration send, you know, construction crews to the Kennedy Center and decide to knock it down, who’s going to stop them?” MS Now’s Eugene Daniels asked. “He knocked down the East Wing, and it’s still unclear if he was legally able to do that.”

“This started back in December of 2025, so I’m a little more hopeful with this because we are in court,” Beatty said.

“He may have thought about doing it when he was ordered to take his name down,” she added. “So I think there is a slight difference.”

The question comes after the Justice Department warned in a court filing Monday that the Kennedy Center could eventually have to be “taken down” if the administration is unable to move forward with a two-year renovation.

The administration has described the building as deteriorating and in need of extensive repairs. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday the planned renovation is expected to cost $257 million.

The plans are tied up in a broader legal battle brought by Beatty over Trump’s efforts to reshape the congressionally established memorial, including adding his name to the building.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that Trump’s name could not be added to the building and ordered the lettering removed, finding that only Congress could change the center’s name.

The Trump-aligned board has since approved a new proposal that would leave the Kennedy Center’s name intact but add an inscription reading “Restored and Renovated by President Donald Trump.”

The Justice Department argued that the new inscription complies with Cooper’s ruling because it does not formally rename the building. Beatty’s attorneys contend the board is trying to get around the earlier ruling.

The center has agreed to hold off on adding the inscription until at least Sept. 8.

But Beatty said she is not dismissing the possibility that Trump could ultimately seek to demolish the building.

“This is a living memorial, the only memorial to an assassinated president that was beloved by many,” she said. “So we’re not taking it lightly.”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed apologizes for comments he made responding to an attack on a Michigan synagogue
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, apologized to the state’s Jewish Democratic Caucus Saturday for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which he tied to Israel’s actions in the Middle East. “My comments may have been misconstrued to justify something I did not mean to justify,” El-Sayed told reporters after he addressed the caucus at a party convention in Lansing. “To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I’m really sorry. That was not my intention.” El-Sayed’s apology was his latest attempt to unify Democrats after a bitter primary in which he defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. He’s eager to push past a series of controversies involving allegations of antisemitism, including his association with controversial commentator Hasan Piker. He faces Republican nominee Mike Rogers in a race that will help determine control of the Senate. In March, a man attacked Temple Israel synagogue in a Detroit suburb, ramming his car into the building and opening fire on a security guard before dying by suicide. The man, Ayman Mohammad Ghazali, had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week prior. In a video response at the time, El-Sayed condemned the attack and added that “hurt people hurt people,” a reference to what happened to Ghazali’s family. Critics accused El-Sayed of justifying Ghazali’s actions. “What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context,” El-Sayed said Saturday, “and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain.”

articles.title: Crianças e adolescentes na internet: propostas dos presidenciáveis | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do g1 nos 13 planos de governo reúne medidas sobre segurança on-line, redes sociais, crimes contra menores, educação digital e saúde mental.
articles.summary: Crianças e adolescentes na internet são foco de propostas sobre segurança digital, saúde mental e combate a crimes nos planos de governo dos 13 candidatos à Presidência.
articles.body:
Candidatos à Presidência da República em 2026: Lula, Flávio, Renan, Caiado, Cury, Zema, Samara, Edmilson Costa, Clariana, Hertz Dias, Marçal, Rui Costa Pimenta e Wilson Grassi — Foto: Montagem g1

Cyberbullying, exploração sexual, discurso de ódio, saúde mental e os riscos das redes sociais. A proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital entrou nos planos de governo dos candidatos à Presidência da República, com propostas que vão do combate a crimes na internet à regulação das plataformas.

O g1 analisou os 13 planos de governo registrados no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para mapear o que os candidatos propõem para tornar a internet mais segura para crianças e adolescentes. O levantamento encontrou medidas de segurança digital, prevenção e repressão a crimes contra menores, educação e cidadania digital e apoio à saúde mental.

Alguns candidatos apresentam propostas específicas para esse tema. Outros tratam da proteção digital dentro de políticas mais amplas voltadas à infância e à juventude.

Veja abaixo o que cada presidenciável propõe para proteger crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital.

O candidato do Avante concentra suas propostas nos impactos das redes sociais sobre a saúde mental de crianças e adolescentes. Entre as medidas sugeridas estão ações educativas nas escolas para estimular o pensamento crítico sobre o uso das redes, discutir os efeitos dos filtros de imagem e prevenir casos de bullying e cyberbullying.

Cury também defende mais transparência e responsabilidade das plataformas digitais em relação a conteúdos que possam prejudicar menores de idade.

Além disso, propõe a criação da chamada "Lei Augusto Cury" (Projeto de Lei nº 5.815/2025). A proposta prevê acompanhamento pediátrico e psicossocial anual para ajudar a proteger crianças contra exploração, automutilação, tráfico e predadores sexuais na internet.

O plano de governo de Clariana Barão afirma que o capítulo "Mulheres e crianças em primeiro lugar" funciona como um eixo orientador para as demais propostas apresentadas pela candidata.

Sobre crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital, o documento cita três frentes de atuação: prevenção de abuso e exploração, promoção de um ambiente digital seguro com educação sobre riscos e busca ativa de crianças fora da escola.

O plano, no entanto, não detalha como essas medidas seriam implementadas.

O candidato do Partido Comunista Brasileiro (PCB) não apresenta propostas específicas para a proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital.

O plano defende uma "forte regulação das Big Techs e redes sociais imperialistas, com ampliação dos investimentos públicos para a criação de redes sociais estatais nacionais", mas não detalha medidas voltadas ao público infantojuvenil.

Para crianças e adolescentes, o documento menciona ações voltadas ao ambiente físico, como fortalecimento de conselhos tutelares, ampliação de creches e orfanatos, incentivo à adoção e combate ao trabalho infantil. Não há propostas específicas para o ambiente on-line.

O candidato do Partido Liberal (PL) não apresenta propostas específicas para a proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital.

Há, no entanto, menções pontuais a crianças, tecnologia e uso de dispositivos digitais. O plano defende o esporte como ferramenta para "tirar a criança da rua e do celular" e propõe ampliar o acesso à robótica e à internet nas escolas, como parte das políticas de educação e inclusão tecnológica.

O documento também aborda a proteção da privacidade e dos dados pessoais de forma mais ampla, ao defender medidas para resguardar as informações de "quem está do outro lado da tela", sem apresentar ações específicas para crianças e adolescentes.

O plano de Hertz Dias tem como foco a soberania tecnológica sob controle dos trabalhadores e faz críticas ao atual modelo de digitalização do ensino.

O candidato não apresenta propostas específicas para a proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital.

O documento também critica o que chama de "projeto da burguesia" de militarização e plataformização das escolas públicas.

O plano de Lula destaca medidas já adotadas pelo governo federal, como a proibição do uso de celulares nas escolas e a criação do Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA) Digital.

O documento propõe aperfeiçoar o ECA Digital e regulamentar o uso de telas conforme a faixa etária. Também prevê ações para promover o uso seguro da tecnologia e regulamentar plataformas de jogos e outros ambientes virtuais.

Além disso, afirma que o "combate à pedofilia continuará prioritário", com punições para casos de exploração sexual infantil e crimes de ódio na internet.

O plano de governo de Pablo Marçal não apresenta propostas específicas ou menções diretas sobre crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital. Contudo, o documento aborda os temas de tecnologia, segurança e infância sob outras perspectivas.

O foco tecnológico voltado para os jovens está na capacitação e na infraestrutura, propondo a garantia de internet em 100% das escolas públicas e o fortalecimento do ensino de computação e inteligência artificial.

O candidato também propõe a criação de um Comando Nacional de Defesa Digital voltado à cibersegurança e proteção de infraestruturas críticas de forma geral, sem recortes específicos para o público infantojuvenil.

O candidato do Missão aborda os temas de tecnologia, regulação e juventude separadamente, fora do tema do público infantojuvenil no ambiente digital. Em suas propostas, Renan Santos se posiciona de forma contrária a regulação da internet ou da mídia que possa reduzir a margem de liberdade de expressão no Brasil.

No tratamento de crianças e adolescentes, o foco do plano está direcionado para a ordem e a autoridade no ambiente escolar físico, não digital. Renan defende a criação de um código de conduta nacional para estudantes com punições objetivas e afirma que as propostas de seu partido exigem uma reavaliação do papel do Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA) para restaurar a disciplina, o respeito à hierarquia e sanar o ambiente escolar.

As propostas de tecnologia voltadas para o público jovem buscam a formação técnica e a retenção de talentos científicos, com foco na ampliação de vagas em cursos de STEM (ciência, tecnologia, engenharia e matemática) e no estímulo à atração de grandes datacenters para transformar o país em um polo de infraestrutura digital

O candidato do Novo concentra suas propostas para infância, juventude e tecnologia no desenvolvimento social físico, na rigidez penal e na oposição à regulação de conteúdos na internet, mas sem propostas que acessem, especificamente, crianças e adolescentes no ambiente online.

O plano adota uma postura firme de liberdade de expressão e se posiciona contra a regulação de plataformas, chegando a propor proibir que as redes sociais realizem a moderação de opiniões ou a exclusão de perfis.

Caiado propõe integrar segurança pública, conselhos tutelares, escolas e Justiça em protocolos unificados de atendimento e investigação, com foco na proteção contra agressões no ambiente digital, recrutamento pelo crime e exploração sexual.

O plano trata a proteção digital de crianças e adolescentes como área de ação integrada, estabelecendo que todas as políticas públicas ligadas à internet e à tecnologia deverão demonstrar impacto orçamentário e social mensurável sobre a infância.

O candidato também defende a consolidação em lei de regras de responsabilidade e transparência para plataformas e mercados digitais, de modo a implementar plenamente a proteção de crianças e adolescentes, protegendo os princípios do Marco Civil da Internet.

Apresenta, em seu plano de governo, uma visão contrária à limitação de ferramentas tecnológicas no ambiente educacional e às regulações da internet. Posiciona-se contra restrições nas escolas, exigindo expressamente o fim da proibição do uso de celulares nas salas de aula.

As propostas do candidato do PCO defendem a liberdade irrestrita de expressão na internet, e se manifesta contra propostas regulatórias como a chamada "Lei Felca".

Não há, no plano de governo de Samara Martins, menções ou propostas específicas voltadas para a proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital. Assim como em outros planos analisados, o documento aborda os temas de infância, juventude, tecnologia e ambiente digital de maneira separada.

As propostas para o público infantojuvenil são centradas em direitos sociais, educação, assistência e segurança no ambiente físico.

Já as propostas tecnológicas do plano têm caráter macroeconômico, com foco na soberania nacional: a candidata defende o fim do monopólio estrangeiro sobre as redes digitais no Brasil e a democratização dos meios de comunicação e da internet.

O plano de governo de Wilson Grassi não apresenta propostas ou menções específicas sobre a proteção de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital.

O candidato trata os temas de infância, juventude e tecnologia de forma separada, em três frentes distintas: educação e juventude no mundo físico (foco em garantir a alfabetização das crianças até o fim do segundo ano, aulas de educação física estruturadas e programas territoriais voltados para a juventude em áreas com maior índice de criminalidade), prevenção de violência e tecnologia e cibersegurança (sem recorte para crianças).

articles.title: Mais de mil bairros de BH e região podem ficar sem água neste domingo  | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a companhia, serão realizadas obras da Cemig, da Secretaria de Estado de Infraestrutura, Mobilidade e Parcerias (SEINFRA) e da Copasa e por isso o abastecimento será interrompido.
articles.summary: A interrupção no abastecimento de água ocorre devido a obras da Copasa, Cemig e Seinfra no Sistema Rio Manso, atingindo 15 cidades da Grande BH neste domingo (30).
articles.body:
Imagem ilustrativa de uma torneira — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

A Copasa informou que neste domingo (30), mais de mil bairros de Belo Horizonte e Região Metropolitana ficarão sem água devido a uma paralisação de unidades que integram o Sistema de Abastecimento de Água Rio Manso.

Segundo a companhia, serão realizadas obras da Cemig, da Secretaria de Estado de Infraestrutura, Mobilidade e Parcerias (SEINFRA) e da Copasa ( veja a lista completa de bairros mais abaixo ).

Em Pedro Leopoldo, estão previstas ações de substituição de bombas do sistema de abastecimento de água, a realização de melhorias no sistema elétrico da unidade de bombeamento e a instalação de registros de manobras na rede de abastecimento.

Para isso, será realizado o desligamento da Linha de Distribuição Igarapé, em Brumadinho, e obras de drenagem urbana em Contagem, com remanejamento de adutoras.

Os serviços devem começar logo pela manhã, por volta das 7h e, durante o período de paralisação, a Copasa recomenda que os moradores utilizem a água das caixas d’água de forma racional, priorizando o consumo essencial.

A normalização ocorrerá de forma gradativa após a conclusão dos serviços, uma vez que é necessário tempo para a recomposição dos níveis dos reservatórios e a pressurização das redes de distribuição.
